So I've gotten in touch with my LBS about getting set up with a touring bike. It'll be great for commuting in the winter, and later I'll be able to take it out for some actual touring. It's going to be a Surly LHT with 26 inch rims. The only things I am absolutely certain that I will want to change are the brakes. I want to swap out the stock cantilever brakes for a set of linear pull V brakes. The clearance will be lower, but the trade-off is that the brakes will have a little more stopping power and they will be easier to service. When I spoke to the owner of the bike shop, he informed me that his distributor also had some 2014 models that they're slightly discounting in order to clear them out. I asked what the differences were between those and the 2015 models, and one of the things he said was that they came with 9 speed rear cassettes whereas the newer 2015 LHT comes with 10 speed rear cassettes. This got me thinking...

Having recently replaced basically the entire drive train on one of my bikes, I'm curious about 2 things: cost, and availability. This is a touring bike, so I might actually have to replace things on it while I am out on a tour, and as such, the most important thing for replacement parts is that they must be easy to locate.

This also got me thinking further about the gears. Do I really need more than 7? The bike I ride now has a 7 speed freewheel and 3 chain rings. I rarely if ever use the inner chain ring. I mostly stick to the middle ring and go up and down on the rear gears as needed, occasionally moving to the large outer front chain ring if I want to pick up some extra speed on a flat stretch or while going downhill. The bike itself weighs over 35 pounds with everything I have on it, which is pretty heavy (it's a very cheap bike so being that heavy is kinda expected), and I often load it up with several pounds of groceries. My other bike is 45 pounds with everything I've put on it, only has 6 gears in the rear, and I rarely use the inner front chain ring on that as well. Where I live is also not very flat, so I'm doing a fair bit of climbing. In my daily rides, I simply have no need for any extra gears in the back.

So I guess what I'm asking is that in terms of cost and availability, what would be the best number of gears to go with for the rear cassette on a touring bike? For the sake of simplicity, should I go with 7? Would 9 or 10 be more of a pain to keep properly indexed? Which is the cheapest to buy cassettes and chains for between 7, 9, and 10? Which is the easiest to find replacements for the chain and cassette between 7, 9, and 10 speeds?

What is your own preference on the number of gears for touring, and what is your opinion for what is best overall?

edit: or should I just go for an internal hub? I never even considered that could be an option for touring. Anyone know anything about these? Is it possible to have an internal rear hub while having more than one usable chain ring at the front? I have not seen any examples of that.
Rear Cassette Gears for Touring: Which is best?

Well, looks like I'm sort of answering my own question.

After extensive searching, it seems like 10 speed is going to be the most commonly available option. Not only that, but it's stronger than 9 speed, at least according to this somewhat unscientific test:

http://www.bikerumor.com/2013/02/19/bikerumor-shimano-chainwear-challenge-the-results/

Unfortunately it's also the most expensive, but I guess you can't have the best of everything.

I think I'd still prefer a seven speed cassette to be honest, since I have more confidence in the durability of the cassettes and chains, and keeping the shifting indexed would be a lot less of a hassle. But I guess that's the tradeoff for a larger range of gears. Maybe I can live with it, even though I don't see myself needing anything more than 7 gears on my daily commutes. For longer rides, I may wind up needing those extra cogs, especially if I've got the bike loaded up with extra weight. Time will tell.

Oh and it turns out that internal hubs require you to have only one front chain ring, so for loaded touring over variable terrain, it's less than ideal. So that's out.
